key_gap: Both sides diagnosed the threshold public good (8 of 12 shifts; benefit 3 to all, cost 1 per shift) and designed the same institution — contingent access / excludability, free endogenous monitoring, graduated sanctions — with the observed 3- and 5-shift seasons read as the one-shot under-provision equilibrium, and an efficiency gap of 36 vs 8. The gap is ordering and ownership: the human opened with the payoff table as the first move and landed the pivotal-marginal logic in one pass ('a shift pays only when I am the exact 8th commitment; the observed failures ARE the equilibrium'); the AI re-derived the same game inside its WHY stage and reached the identical institution with scaffolding overhead, stating the core insight later and more cautiously.
learning_signal: For recurring under-provision, convert character claims into payoff structure before prescribing: (1) write the game first — threshold, individual benefit, cost, one-shot vs repeated — and compute the one-shot equilibrium; if contribution is pivotal-only, under-provision IS the equilibrium and observed 'laziness' is equilibrium behavior, not a culture problem; (2) price the efficiency gap (full-provision benefit vs cost) as the argument for institutionalizing; (3) the fix must change payoffs, not rhetoric: excludability (contingent access converts a public good into a club good and makes contribution the price of entry), monitoring that is endogenous and free, graduated sanctions; (4) audit the institution's own failure modes — measurement (defined, logged units), sanction credibility (compliant-first sequencing makes exclusion self-enforcing), collusion — and close at least one concretely; (5) then and only then decide to adopt.
suggested_improvement: Add a 'game-write-down' gate to the WHY stage for public-goods / resource-allocation decisions: (a) before generating alternatives, require the payoff table (cost / benefit / threshold / horizon) and the stated one-shot equilibrium; treat the observed failure pattern as the equilibrium to be explained, not as evidence of motive; (b) give every candidate rule a mechanism test — does it make contribution a best response, does it need exogenous enforcement or can it self-enforce, who pays for monitoring?; (c) require an institution failure-mode pass (measurement, sanction credibility, collusion) with at least one closed loop before adoption; (d) let 'moral appeal' enter the alternative set but require it to pass the same payoff gate — it fails unless it changes the game.

key_gap: The pure style correctly saw the free-rider element (a skipping household saves 2h while the street stays mostly protected) and answered with canonical mechanism design — acclamation ratification, sign-in sheet at the barrier, post-event fines — adapting the machinery to the clock rather than discarding it. It never priced stand-up cost against the problem's lifetime (36h: draft, ratify, appoint a neutral party that does not exist in-window), never noticed its sanctions cannot fire before the crest, and ignored crowding-out (fines converting intrinsic neighbor reciprocity into a fee transaction) plus the 6-eyes monitoring already present. The AI ran a horizon test — stand-up cost > problem lifetime, zero in-window enforcement, redundant monitoring — and selected direct mobilization (one call per household, roll-call of shifts, all hands at dawn, departing families fill tonight), naming the meta-lesson 'the norm is the institution.'
learning_signal: Institutional machinery has a cost function in group size, horizon, and transaction costs; before designing a mechanism, run the stand-up test: (1) can the institution (rule + monitoring + sanctions + appeals) be operational within the decision horizon? if stand-up cost > problem lifetime, the mechanism is the failure mode; (2) check in-window enforcement capacity — a sanction that cannot fire before the deadline deters nothing; (3) run the redundancy audit: when n is small and observation is mutual (six neighbors), the formal monitoring layer adds cost and no information; (4) check crowding-out — converting intrinsic, reciprocity-based mobilization into a fine-based transaction can lower rather than raise effort; (5) the cheap local action (one call, roll-call, existing norms) IS an institution — name it as such instead of contrasting 'no institution' vs 'institution' — and defer formalization to when the horizon allows it to pay (a post-crisis standing plan).
suggested_improvement: Add a 'horizon / stand-up gate' to the WHAT or WHY stage for any proposed mechanism: (a) before endorsing a rule, compute stand-up cost (steps x time) vs problem lifetime and in-window enforcement capacity (can the sanction actually fire before the deadline?); (b) run the redundancy audit (is observation already complete without the machinery? does the group's reciprocity already sanction?); (c) run the crowd-out check (does monetizing the act change its meaning and reduce intrinsic effort?); (d) include the cheap local action as a first-class alternative with its own stand-up cost (minutes vs days) rather than treating 'informal' as 'no solution'; (e) if the problem recurs, schedule the formal institution for after the crisis, when its stand-up cost amortizes.
